title: Twenty-One Million Dollars for Burnt Contraband: The Opium Traders’ Loss Becomes China’s Sovereign Debt

extractionLoop.stage1_upfrontSkim: The Bengal opium monopoly the East India Company built after the Diwani is sold at Calcutta auction and carried to Canton by private firms — Jardine, Matheson & Co. and Dent & Co. the largest — who take the margin on a trade Chinese law prohibits and British law does not reach.
extractionLoop.stage2_structuralCompromise: When Commissioner Lin Zexu confiscates the 20,283 chests at Canton in March 1839, Superintendent Charles Elliot takes them into Crown hands first and promises the holders that the British government will make the loss good. A private stock of contraband becomes, in a single administrative act, a claim on the Treasury.
extractionLoop.stage3_informationFog: The claim is argued in London as a question of national honour and the liberty of British subjects, not as compensation for a drug cargo. Sir James Graham’s censure motion of 7 April 1840 keeps the Commons three nights on the imprudence of ministers; the expedition sails either way.
extractionLoop.stage4_monopolyWindfall: The Treaty of Nanking charges the whole bill to the Chinese state: six million dollars for the destroyed opium, three million for Hong-merchant debts, twelve million for the expedition itself, twenty-one million in all on a schedule to 1845, plus Hong Kong in perpetuity and five ports opened to British trade.
extractionLoop.stage5_merseyWhitewash: No British party pays. The indemnity is settled on China as sovereign debt, the traders are made whole for a cargo their own government had surrendered, and the treaty-port system becomes the template for the next century of forced-trade settlements.

closedLoopRatchet.inheritedFramework: The East India Company’s Bengal revenue and opium monoculture, and the Crown’s habit of standing behind chartered traders’ losses.
closedLoopRatchet.newFrameworkCreated: The gunboat indemnity: a state-to-state treaty that converts a private trading loss into sovereign debt with a payment schedule, secured by ceded territory and treaty ports.
closedLoopRatchet.closedLoopRecirculation: The firms whose stock was surrendered are paid out of the indemnity; the indemnity is collected from Chinese customs revenue; the ports opened to collect it carry the next decade of the same trade.

decoyVsLedger.viralDecoy: A clash of civilisations over free trade and diplomatic protocol — an arrogant empire refusing to open its ports, met by a Britain defending the rights of its merchants abroad.
decoyVsLedger.whyDecoyFails: The treaty itself names the consideration. Article IV pays six million dollars ‘as the value of the Opium which was delivered up at Canton in the month of March, 1839’ — the destroyed contraband is written into the settlement as a priced item, before the war costs in Article VI.
decoyVsLedger.documentedLedger: Elliot took the traders’ opium into government hands against a promise of compensation; the Commons debated and narrowly declined to censure the ministry on 7 April 1840; and the Treaty of Nanking recovered the whole sum — twenty-one million dollars under Articles IV to VII — from the Chinese state, with Hong Kong and five treaty ports attached.

citations.title: Treaty of Nanking (29 August 1842), Articles IV–VII, in W. F. Mayers (ed.), Treaties Between the Empire of China and Foreign Powers (Shanghai, 1877), p. 1
citations.quoteOrFact: Art. IV: "The Emperor of China agrees to pay the sum of Six Millions of Dollars, as the value of the Opium which was delivered up at Canton in the month of March, 1839, as a ransom for the lives of Her Britannic Majesty’s Superintendent and Subjects". Art. V adds three millions for insolvent Hong-merchants’ debts, Art. VI twelve millions for the expedition’s expenses, and Art. VII fixes the total at "Twenty-one Millions of Dollars" payable by the end of 1845. Read from the Internet Archive full text of the 1877 Mayers compilation, whose table of contents files the Nanking treaty of 1842 at page 1.

citations.title: War With China, HC Deb 07 April 1840 vol 53 cc669–748 (Historic Hansard)
citations.quoteOrFact: Historic Hansard’s transcript of the first night of the Commons debate on the China war, opened by Sir James Graham, who moves that the interruption of relations with China was owing mainly to the "want of foresight and precaution" of the Government’s advisers. The page is the debate itself; the division that defeated the motion falls on the sitting of 9 April and is not on this page.
